title: Lunch and the check
goal: Order a full meal, ask for the check, pay, and use the verb *querer*.

dialogs.title: Diálogo — La comida del mediodía
dialogs.intro: Lunch, the main meal of the day. Two people sit down, order, and ask for the check.

lines.speaker: Camarero:
lines.id: Good afternoon. A table for two?
lines.literal: good afternoons. a table for two?

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Sí, por favor. ¿Hay menú del día?
lines.id: Yes, please. Is there a set menu today?
lines.literal: yes, please. there-is menu of-the day?

lines.speaker: Camarero:
lines.text: Sí. De primero, sopa o ensalada. De segundo, pollo o pescado.
lines.id: Yes. For the first course, soup or salad. For the second, chicken or fish.
lines.literal: yes. of first, soup or salad. of second, chicken or fish.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Para mí, ensalada y pollo, por favor.
lines.id: For me, salad and chicken, please.
lines.literal: for me, salad and chicken, please.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Yo quiero sopa. Y de segundo, pescado.
lines.id: I'd like soup. And for the second course, fish.
lines.literal: I I-want soup. and of second, fish.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Una botella de agua, por favor. Sin gas.
lines.id: A bottle of water, please. Still.
lines.literal: a bottle of water, please. without gas.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: Great! Excuse me, where's the restroom?
lines.literal: how good! pardon (polite), where is the bathroom?

lines.speaker: Camarero:
lines.id: At the back, on the right.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: La cuenta, por favor. ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?
lines.id: The check, please. Can I pay by card?
lines.literal: the bill, please. one can to-pay with card?

lines.speaker: Camarero:
lines.id: Yes, of course. That's twenty euros.

notes: **Menú del día** is an institution in Spain: a first course, a second course, bread, a drink and dessert for one fixed price, at lunchtime only. Don't confuse it with *la carta* — that's the full list of dishes, what English calls "the menu".
**Del = de + el.** *El menú del día*, not *de el día*. This merge is required, not a matter of style.
**Para mí** = "for me". Note the ´ on *mí* — without it, *mi* means "my". After a preposition, the pronoun changes form: *para mí*, *para ti*, *para él*.

**Quiero vs quisiera.** *Quiero sopa* is perfectly fine among friends or when ordering quickly; *quisiera* is softer still. What's really rude is just naming the dish with nothing else — that's true everywhere.
**Sin gas / con gas** = still or sparkling water. In Spain, *agua* in a restaurant almost always comes in a bottle and is rarely free.
**¿Dónde está…?** uses *estar*, not *ser*, because you're asking about location. The difference is covered fully in Unit 11; for now: **location always takes *estar***.
**Perdone / perdona** = "excuse me" to interrupt someone — the first is polite, the second informal. Don't confuse it with *lo siento*, which is a real apology.
**¿Se puede…?** = "can one…? / is it OK to…?" without saying who. A handy all-purpose pattern: *¿se puede pagar con tarjeta?*, *¿se puede fumar aquí?*

grammars.title: Querer (to want) and hay (there is)
body: *Querer* is one of the verbs that **change inside**, not just at the end: the *e* in the stressed syllable becomes *ie*. The same pattern turns up later in *tener*, *empezar* and *preferir*.
after: *Hay* stands outside every table: it has no other forms, no subject, and means "there is" or "there are". *Hay una mesa libre* (there's one free table), *hay tres mesas libres* (there are three free tables).
The negative is just *no hay*: *no hay pescado hoy* — there's no fish today. You'll hear this a lot in small cafés late in the afternoon.

blocks.title: El agua — a tricky word
items: *Agua* is **feminine**, but in the singular it takes *el*: *el agua*, not *la agua*. The reason is purely sound — *la agua* sounds like one stuttered word.
The proof is that its adjective stays feminine: *el agua fría* (cold water), not *frío*. And in the plural everything goes back to normal: *las aguas*.
Other words treated the same way: *el aula* (classroom), *el hambre* (hunger), *el águila* (eagle). Same feature: feminine, starting with a stressed **a** sound.

blocks.title: Mealtimes that shift
items: A Spanish breakfast is very light: coffee and toast, often standing at the bar. The big meal is lunch, around 2-3 p.m., and dinner doesn't start until 9 p.m. A restaurant open at 6 p.m. is almost certainly a tourist restaurant.
*Tapas* are small portions served with drinks. In some cities — Granada is the most famous — tapas come free with every drink you order.
*La propina* (the tip) isn't required or expected the way it is in the US. Leaving some change or rounding up the bill is seen as friendly.
You have to ask for the check; a waiter who brings it unasked is seen as hurrying guests out. *La cuenta, por favor* — or raise your hand and draw a little square in the air.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of *querer* (*quiero*, *quieres*, *quiere*).
Put the words in order to make a correct Spanish sentence.

answers: La cuenta, por favor. — ¿Hay menú del día? — Una botella de agua. — ¿Dónde está el baño? — Nada más, gracias.
Can I pay by card? — There's no fish today. — Dessert is included. — For here or to go? — That's four euros fifty.
